summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening at Puerto Rico's airports follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched. Prosthetics, including breast forms, are treated as medically necessary equipment rather than liquids: they are exempt from the three-liquid rule and are allowed through the checkpoint after screening. Guidance for trans travellers advises packing strategies that reduce the likelihood of invasive searches.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for that care, and set penalties of up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of medical licences for doctors who violate the ban. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The care law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment, but the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage remains partial. The 2013 law that passed (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered by it. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Under Executive Order 14168, which directs United States federal agencies to recognise only two sexes, the Bureau of Prisons houses transgender inmates by sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity, a rule that governs any federal custody in Puerto Rico. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order contravenes the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by individual safety assessment.
tangentialFactors:
Puerto Rico's care restrictions place it at the extreme end of the United States patchwork: the report documenting the 2025 law describes it as the most extreme care restriction among United States jurisdictions, which is the comparison frame a trans visitor from the mainland should carry.

Other United States territories and states face the same federal document, screening and custody rules described above, so the federal layer of this assessment transfers directly; what is distinctive about Puerto Rico is the additional local restriction on care for people under 21 and the narrower local anti-discrimination statute.

Sexual conduct law was settled against local precedent: Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002, and after the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

LGBT rights groups in Puerto Rico have repeatedly defeated religious-freedom pairings with conversion-therapy measures, and marriage equality reached the territory through federal rather than local litigation, the pattern by which several protections described here arrived.
localsOnly:
Residents under 21 cannot lawfully obtain gender-affirming care in Puerto Rico since the July 2025 statute, and the statute's vague drafting exposes doctors and parents who facilitate hormone treatment or surgery to prosecution even where the conduct was previously routine. Departmental campaigns against trans-affirming care are part of the enacted text.

Conversion-therapy regulation has been repeatedly blocked. In March 2019 the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the Puerto Rico House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors, despite Senate passage and governor support; Senator Zoe Laboy, a co-sponsor, publicly dissented. In April 2019 Governor Rossello announced a pairing of SB1253, framed as clarifying religious freedom principles, with SB1254, a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption for clergy; LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open doors to discrimination, arguing the religious-freedom carve-out licensed refusal of service on orientation and gender-identity grounds. On 13 June 2019 the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both bills amid sustained opposition.

A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018.

Household protections are broader than public-accommodation protections: in 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Marriage equality in Puerto Rico was secured through federal court. Four same-sex couples joined the federal lawsuit filed in March 2014 (the Ada Conde Vidal case), with Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas intervening; among the couples, one had married in Canada in 2007 and another in New York in 2012, and a former National Guard member was among the plaintiffs.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy on transgender-inmate housing, no special unit, and no judicial ruling on the point was located in the sources; the custody picture rests entirely on the federal order and on ACLU reporting.

The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced a legal challenge to the July 2025 care ban, but no filed case, ruling or injunction appears in the inventory, so the ban's litigation status is unresolved.

Restroom and facility access for trans people, and the procedure and fees for changing gender markers on Puerto Rico-issued identity documents, are not addressed by any source here; the document picture is limited to the federal travel-document position.

Whether the under-21 care ban applies to adults aged 18 to 20 who are visiting rather than residing in Puerto Rico is not stated in the sources reviewed, as is enforcement practice against non-residents.
